#1081. Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter

Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.

With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.

Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.

"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.

Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.

While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.

Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.

With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.

"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.

That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

Martin Odegaard has defined Arsenal under Mikel Arteta - but could be about to depart the club after five years

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard is at risk of leaving Arsenal for Bayern Munich.

This year, the Norwegian became the first Gunners skipper to lift a Premier League title since Patrick Vieira in 2004, when Arsenal brought the trophy back to N5 in May, cementing himself in the minds of many fans as a genuine legend of the club.

But Odegaard now 27 and approaching the final year of his current contract next summer, manager Mikel Arteta has a decision to make over whether he builds his next team around a playmaker who has been so influential for him over the past five years.

Odegaard has been one of Arteta's greatest signings, joining the Gunners initially on loan from Real Madrid before Arsenal triggered a deal worth around £30 million and build a midfield around the former wonderkid.

While the 27-year-old has been back to his best this season, however, the last 18-24 months have been difficult for Odegaard, with injury and poor form opening the door to Eberechi Eze to stake a claim in the first team – and some suggesting that the Norway captain is less of a No.10 and more of a No.8 that the Gunners don't need alongside Bruno Guimaraes and Declan Rice in the engine room.

Sky Deutschland have reported via Sport Witness that Odegaard can “envision a future move” to Bayern Munich, with the Bavarians having already discussed a move for the star.

Arsenal, meanwhile, are working on a contract extension for a player who is still key to Arteta's side both in and out of possession, as shown in the early stages of this season.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While the champions have held informal talks with the star over remaining at the club, it's now being reported that Arsenal “would be open to selling” their skipper for the first time, should they fail to tie him down before the end of the summer.

This marks the first time in Odegaard's Arsenal career that it's been reported that the club are genuinely looking to cash in on the player – even throughout the injury troubles and more fervent criticism online of the player's role within Arteta's system.

The Basque boss has built around the midfielder since his first full season, with Odegaard almost untouchable, despite options such as Fabio Vieira, Emile Smith Rowe, Ethan Nwaneri and the signing of Eze all challenging for a spot in Arteta's midfield.

For now, Sport Witness claims that “It looks like his camp are using Bayern Munich’s timid interest to put pressure on Arsenal to secure an improved deal for the renewal.”

The Drammen native will be 30 years old when Arteta's current deal at the Emirates Stadium comes to an end.

Odegaard is valued at €80 million by Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Liverpool this weekend as Premier League action continues.

The Glazer family are understood to be angry with INEOS after disastrous start to 2026/27

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United's majority owners are angry about Jim Ratcliffe's running of the club, according to reports.

Man United are owned primarily by the Glazer family, with brothers Joel and Avram holding the position of co-chairmen despite the extremely hands-off nature of their involvement.

The Glazers handed the running of the football side of United to INEOS when Ratcliffe and his company secured a shareholding of more than a quarter of the club, an agreement that has failed to get the Red Devils out of a rut.

Ratcliffe initially bought a 25 percent share in December 2023 and INEOS assumed control of United's football operations. Since then, enormous investment in the playing side has led to continued underperformance.

United finished third in the Premier League last season but have been subject to constant doubts over coaching and behind-the-scenes battles about technical directors and managers.

The Glazers, who own the remainder of the Old Trafford club, are understood to be less than satisfied about Ratcliffe's leadership and running of United's football business, according to the Daily Mail.

"It’s a travesty and not what they expected or were promised," a source told Ian Herbert. They have never run the club this way."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Mail reports that a decision to sell Manchester United could be on the cards for the Glazers in the long run, with their interest in the club as low as ever and United fans' opinion of them rarely improving above outright contempt.

"The $6bn (£4.5bn) valuation which the Glazers put on the club when seeking a buyer, four years ago, is looking more unrealistic than ever," reports Herbert.

"The Glazers control any sale. A clause in their deal with Ratcliffe, completed in 2024, lets them force him out of his 28 percent stake – and out of the entire landscape – if they sell the club to a third party, without him having any say, unless he can match that offer and buy the entire club himself.

"Whatever displeasure they might feel, they can’t buy back Ratcliffe’s piece of the United pie. But from next February, Ratcliffe will be powerless to stop them selling the entire club for a price lower than the $33 (£25) a share he paid for his chunk."

United's fortunes on the pitch are no more serene than developments behind closed doors. Having appointed interim head coach Michael Carrick on a permanent basis at the end of last season, the Red Devils have won just two of their 12 fixtures in all competitions this season.

Carrick's team have dropped into the bottom five in the Premier League table and two senior players have broken ranks in recent weeks to criticise either technical director Jason Wilcox or the tactics of the head coach.

United face Chelsea in the early Premier League match on Saturday.

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton's Carabao Cup tie over a breach of club discipline

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In May 2019, Jack Grealish climbed the steps at Wembley in a pair of tatty and worn-out football boots to rubberstamp his team's return to the Premier League.

Aston Villa had beaten Derby County in the Championship play-off final, their second attempt in as many years, and their promotion was regarded as a do-or-die moment for a club that had lost its way.

Grealish captained Villa through a record-breaking run of wins to qualify for the play-offs. Like his manager, Dean Smith, he is a Villa supporter to his core. He was on top of the world, tipped for a distinguished England career and set to be every bit the phenom in the Premier League that he was in the second tier.

As Grealish and his teammates lifted the trophy in Wembley's royal box, its rim nicked his eyebrow. This is Jack Grealish: Already beloved by his people for years, as naturally talented as any English footballer since Paul Gascoigne, a scintillating player and emerging leader, and a self-saboteur.

After steering Villa to the Premier League after three years away, Grealish flourished in the top flight and kept them there. He became a £100 million player when he left for Manchester City, where he played his part in winning the treble in 2022/23 but had to sacrifice the individual style that made him extraordinary.

And he was extraordinary. As humdrum as he was at City by comparison, as unremarkable as his two loan spells at Everton have been, Villa supporters can look back on his performances and lament a player who could have been an all-time great at the club he loved but chose a different path.

Sadly, that road gave Grealish the trophies and international recognition he craved but left him vulnerable to the self-destructive streak that occasionally made him headline news in his years at Villa.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Outside that cocoon he seems to have lost his way. Everton supporters will find it difficult to forgive his most recent transgression. Grealish was left out of the Toffees' squad for this week's Carabao Cup fixture against Newcastle United because of a 'breach of club discipline' that's widely reported to have been an unauthorised absence from training.

David Moyes' team selection when the same teams meet again in the Premier League on Monday night will reveal the depth of feeling about the matter within the club; for some supporters, failings of professionalism cross a line.

Grealish, at 31, faces a fight to win back a place in the team and the backing of supporters at a club with no vested interest in his future beyond May, and he only has himself to blame.

Everton and Moyes have to protect their interests and ensuring that disciplinary matters are dealt with is key to keeping a dressing room functioning properly. Premier League footballers are extremely wealthy young men and Grealish, considered too expensive for Villa to take on loan last summer, has made a fortune.

The minimum standard expected in exchange for that is rather higher than simply showing up for work. Falling short of that level isn't acceptable for any player and Everton were forced to take action, but it can also be indicative of a player's need for support.

The reasons for Grealish's breach of club discipline will never be made public by Everton, nor should they.

Nobody but Grealish and those closest to him will know the details behind the tall tales and photographs that have followed him throughout his career. Only Grealish will know his own mind; speculation about his life is unfair and irresponsible.

Whatever Grealish's reasons for doing what he did to trigger such a clear reaction from Everton this week, the act itself confirms that his story has become a cautionary one.

He has all the ability in the world and enough style and confidence to shine on the biggest stages football has to offer. He became the cornerstone of his own club and delivered tangible success beyond anything any other local boy had achieved for generations.

As players of that ilk make their way in the game, it's easy to forget that they're people too. Some will have struggles and battles to fight away from football, and some will ultimately let their professionalism slip no matter how capable they are on the pitch.

Supporters can view that in any way they wish. Many will simply look at the wages a player receives and have very little sympathy.

Football clubs, and football as a whole, must take a more serious approach. Fans don't owe players anything but football certainly does. If nothing else, the game's duty of care to its players should help them make the right decisions to fulfil their promise.

#1076. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1074. World Cup 2034: Does Saudi Arabia shelving Neom Stadium spell trouble?

Since winning the right to hold the 2034 World Cup unopposed, Saudi Arabia has been pulling away from sport. With reports that its most ambitious stadium project will be abandoned, what does this mean for the World Cup?

It was billed as "the most unique stadium in the world," a key pillar of Saudi Arabia's World Cup 2034 plans. But now Neom Stadium, part of the kingdom's ambitious aims to build a 170-kilometer-long (111-mile) city in the desert known as The Line, looks set to be scrapped, with the broader project scaled back significantly.

A recent Reuters report said the stadium, which according to the country's bid book was going to be "350 meters (1,148 feet) above ground" and have "stunning vistas, and a roof created from the city itself," would no longer be built for the tournament, where it was to host a quarterfinal and several other games.

Observers of the gulf country saw this coming.

"When I was in Saudi Arabia in December there were already plenty of signals that the whole Neom project was being put on the back burner, if not abandoned altogether," F. Gregory Gause III, a regional expert from the Middle East Institute think tank in Washington D.C., told DW.

"I see it as part of a general reevaluation of their fiscal situation, both in light of the oil market before the current war and in light of the damage that the war is doing. The drawback from sports commitments is just part of a more general reassessment of priorities in the current, more straitened, situation."

Saudi Arabia's sports splurge that saw players like Cristiano Ronaldo join the country's football league and the kingdom invest in all sorts of sports in myriad ways has slowed dramatically. The country pulled funding for the multibillion dollar LIV Golf as well as events in snooker, tennis and rugby and also withdrew from ambitious plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games in Neom.

Sports had formed a key part of Saudi Arabia's Project 2030, which aimed to diversify the country's economy away from oil and increase its soft power. But Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Saudi-government operated Public Investment Fund (PIF), which also owns Premier League football club Newcastle United, said earlier this year that the PIF was "reassessing its priorities" amid war in the region.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The impact of the war has not only made the economic rationalization more important, but it's also accelerated the desire to rethink some of these projects in the sense that Neom is now being repurposed as an industrial center on the Red Sea, which has obviously assumed much greater urgency since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked," Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, author of "Kingdom of Football: Saudi Arabia and the Remaking of World Soccer," told DW.

There are, Coates Ulrichsen continued, clear parallels with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where plans to build 12 stadiums resulted in only eight being used at the tournament. The Arab Spring uprising arrived shortly after the bid was accepted by FIFA and, though it didn't impact the country directly, it destabilized the region both politically and economically.

Neither Saudi Arabia's World Cup organizing authority or Sports Ministry has responded to questions from DW about whether we may again see fewer stadiums than the planned 15 for the 2034 World Cup, which could feature 64 teams.

"We're seeing the same obviously with Saudi Arabia now," said Coates Ulrichsen, who is also a fellow for the Middle East at Rice University in the US.

"[FIFA President] Gianni Infantino announced Saudi would be the only bidder on the 4th of October 2023. Three days later was October 7th, so within three days, the region was effectively in flames," he said.

Since then, there has been the Israel-US war against Iran, while Houthi attacks continue to hit Saudi Arabia as part of the conflict in Yemen, meaning that: "This whole hosting cycle is taking place against a backdrop of considerable uncertainty and kind of real tension."

But though the scope and cost of it may be reduced, Saudi Arabia's softening commitment to sport will not likely apply so firmly to the biggest sporting event in the world, said Gause.

"I think it continues to be a major priority, because of its global importance and because the Saudis will want to do at least as well, if not outshine, Qatar's hosting earlier."

Relations between Saudi Arabia and Qatar have improved since an agreement in 2021 but the pair remain regional rivals, something Coates Ulrichsen agrees will spur the 2034 hosts on.

As such, the 2034 tournament will still likely be a high-end affair, with Saudi Arabia building most stadiums from scratch. But, said Coates Ulrichsen, it may look somewhat different to what was planned.

"The fact that at least the Saudis were able to host a big event with 60,000 people in the stadiums, full stadiums without any security concerns [the Gulf Cup football final which they won this week] is a good sign," he said.

The regional expert thinks more matches could end up being hosted in the two biggest Saudi cities, Riyadh and Jeddah. This may be at the expense of some venues nearer the east coast such as Al Khobar or Al Ahsa. These are separated from Iran by the Persian Gulf, which includes the Strait of Hormuz, and could be reconsidered depending on the state of political affairs.

Saudi Arabia host football's Asian Cup in January, which Coates Ulrichsen thinks will be an "early test of whether that is viable to have a weeks-long major tournament under these conditions."

With nearly eight years until the World Cup, the political and economic situation in the country is difficult to predict. While the supposed shelving of Neom Stadium and general Saudi sporting withdrawal poses questions of commitment more broadly, it appears the World Cup show will go on. But probably not quite as billed.

#1071. Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn

The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement. Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.

During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

"Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.

This article was written by Andrey Gorezky, translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal and Tenzin Sekhon.

Bayern Munich striker and England captain Harry Kane has addressed talk of further individual accolades after scooping the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Kane became the first English winner of football's biggest individual award since Michael Owen in 2001 when he was given the Ballon d'Or at the end of a glitzy ceremony on Monday evening. The last Bayern player to be recognised as the world's best was Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981.

The 33-year-old was voted top of the football pops after scoring 61 times in 51 appearances in all competitions last season. He led England to the semi-finals of the World Cup and collected his second consecutive Bundesliga title.

Speaking after the first time he laced up his boots as the official best footballer on the planet, Kane gave a typically measured response to suggestions he could be in line to become a knight of the realm as England's fifth Ballon d'Or winner.

"If it happens it'll be incredible, and something I'll be massively proud of. But I don't want to get too carried away. It would sound good, but I'd feel weird everyone calling me Sir. So we'll just keep it as Harry for now."

The England captain is bound to be the subject of political and royal attention whether he wants it or not.

"What a fantastic achievement and so deserved," the Prince posted on Instagram on Monday night. "A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments."

Kane is the kind of professional who will be more openly focused on winning matches and league titles than picking up individual pots, but being rewarded for scoring goals is surely a dream come true for a striker obsessed with goals.

Kane has scored plenty of them. He left Tottenham Hotspur as the second-highest scorer in the Premier League. Only Alan Shearer scored more than Kane's 213 Premier League goals and it took him many more goals to do it.

England's captain is also their record scorer and will become their most-capped player next month when he picks up his 126th cap to go with a shiny pair of European golden shoes.

Kane will have both feet back on terra firm when Bayern Munich take on Borussia Dortmund on Saturday. The teams are locked together on points at the top of the Bundesliga.

#1069. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#1066. 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year

Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around 1 million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added.

"It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment," said Raiser

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

This article was originally written in German.

The Rossoneri are European royalty but they are being left behind - and there may be no way back

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There was a buzz on the south coast of England as a Premier League underdog playing in Europe for the first time prepared to welcome the mighty AC Milan.

On a night that was already a pinch-me moment for the home fans, excitement turned to disbelief as their side went 2-0 up against the seven-time European champions - only for the Italian giants to burst the bubble with two late goals in a 2-2 draw.

Because that Milan team that faced Portsmouth 18 years ago was very different to the one that lost 3-0 to Bournemouth in the Europa League last week. In fact, those two trips to the south coast serve as a barometer of the decline of the Rossoneri.

Looking back now, it is incredible to see how many superstars graced the Fratton Park turf during that UEFA Cup tie in November 2008.

Dida, Gennaro Gattuso, Kaka, Filippo Inzaghi and Andriy Shevchenko all started the game, with Clarence Seedorf, Ronaldinho and Alexandre Pato coming off the bench. Ronaldinho scored a brilliant free-kick to halve the deficit, before Inzaghi snaffled an equaliser in stoppage time. Oh, and Carlo Ancelotti was their manager.

Milan had reached three of the previous six Champions League finals, and eight across the previous two decades. When it came to European royalty, they were on a par with anyone.

While the visit of the Serie A giants would have created a similar buzz in Bournemouth as it did in Portsmouth 18 years earlier, the side that played at the Vitality Stadium was a pale imitation of the one that lined up at Fratton Park.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Whereas the team that drew with Pompey was full of superstars, the only genuinely world-class player in Milan's squad last Thursday was Luka Modric, an unused substitute who turned 41 in September. The starting line-up included English trio Fikayo Tomori, Ruben Loftus-Cheek and Omari Hutchinson, who all left the Premier League - two permanently and the latter on loan from Nottingham Forest - in search of more game-time.

The truth is that Milan cannot attract world-class players at their peak anymore. They haven’t been a force in Europe for nearly two decades, reaching the Champions League quarter-finals just twice since they last lifted the trophy in 2007.

The iconic badge and red-and-black shirt are their only link with the great Milan teams of yesteryear. Even the San Siro, one of world football's most prestigious stadiums, will soon be demolished, severing another connection with the past.

European football is poorer for it, because for many years Milan had an aura that few clubs could match.

This is the club of Arrigo Sacchi, the 4-0 demolition of Barcelona in the 1994 Champions League final, George Weah’s solo goal against Verona, the imperious defensive partnership of Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi (and the long-standing myth about their goals-against record), plus many more iconic moments, matches and individuals.

This is the club who were front and centre of Serie A in its 1990s heyday, when millions of British football fans fell in love with the league through the cult TV show Football Italia.

So, what went wrong? As with many things, the answer comes down to money.

Two days before Ancelotti’s side faced Portsmouth in 2008, Bournemouth drew 0-0 at home to Morecambe in League Two in front of 3,068 fans. The Cherries began that season on -17 points and at one point were reportedly five minutes from liquidation, before eventually escaping relegation under Eddie Howe.

It is in that context that Bournemouth beating Milan is a fairy-tale, but only in that context. Because when you compare the two clubs in 2026, there is no reason why the Cherries should not beat Milan.

The Rossoneri are flying high in Serie A while Bournemouth are in the bottom half of the Premier League, but that is largely irrelevant due to the financial muscle of the English top flight, which boasts a domestic TV rights deal that dwarfs its rivals.

According to Transfermarkt, the market value of Bournemouth’s squad is €624m (roughly £522m), whereas Milan’s is €503.2m (£421m). The Rossoneri have the fourth-most valuable squad in Serie A but would be 14th in the Premier League, three places below the Cherries.

The financial advantage is laid bare in the 2026 Deloitte Football Money League, which ranks the highest revenue-generating clubs in the world. Milan placed 15th with an annual revenue of €410.4m (£344m), below seven Premier League clubs - the ‘Big Six’ of Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea, as well as Aston Villa.

Bournemouth were 26th with a revenue of €218.5m (£183m), but the fact they were only the 13th-highest Premier League club shows the financial power of the English top flight. In terms of Serie A teams, only Inter Milan (11th), the Rossoneri and Juventus (16th) placed higher than the Cherries.

The top four sides in the Money League were Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain, followed by the Premier League’s ‘Big Six’. This encapsulates the balance of power in European football: you have those four superclubs, then the Premier League, then everyone else.

The Champions League is a case in point, with Real, Barca, Bayern and PSG sharing 12 of the past 16 titles and ‘Big Six’ clubs winning the other four. In the past two seasons, Premier League sides have won both the Europa League and Conference League, too.

That is why Milan’s defeat by Bournemouth should not have shocked anyone. Some will see it as a positive that historically ‘small’ clubs like the Cherries can beat giants like Milan, but in reality this only applies to Premier League teams. Barring the odd exception, a club of Bournemouth’s size in any other league would not be able to assemble the same quality of squad.

One of those exceptions is Como, who were on the other side of an Anglo-Italian giant-killing when they thumped Manchester United 4-1 in the Champions League 24 hours earlier. United are a mess, but they have the financial clout to become a force once again. You cannot confidently say the same about Milan.

The Rossoneri are not the only multiple European champions who are a shadow of their former selves - just ask Ajax, Benfica and Juventus. However, the financial landscape has changed so much that there may be no way back.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#1064. Diego Maradona Jnr on life as the son of a footballing icon

Growing up as the offspring of Maradona wasn’t easy, but after winning his dad’s heart and enjoying success in beach soccer, the Neapolitan explains why he’s found peace

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During the summer of 1986, babies named after Diego Armando Maradona were nothing unusual in Naples. In his first two years living below Mount Vesuvius, El Pibe de Oro had transformed Napoli from a mid-table side into Serie A title challengers – oh, and he’d just single-handedly won the World Cup for Argentina, too.

The best footballer on the planet, he was worshipped by millions. In the week after the World Cup Final, 5.5 per cent of all babies born in Argentina were named Diego, a fourfold increase from previously. One suspects the figure in southern Italy wasn’t altogether dissimilar.

“Diego represented so much for us – he was one of us, he was the God of Football here in Naples,” explains Antonio ‘Bostik’ Esposito, the head of Napoli’s ultras back then, speaking with a hoarse voice shaped by a thousand cigarettes. “He’s the greatest footballer in history. He was superhuman.”

Today, Bostik runs a bar in the Largo Maradona, a spot in Napoli’s Quartieri Spagnoli district that’s home to a giant mural of Diego, plus a shrine to the great man with shirts and flowers, as well as stalls selling a whole host of paraphernalia. Before the mural was painted in 1990, this place was a drug den, frequented only by young people eager to forget their complicated life. Now, it’s visited by tourists and pilgrims from far and wide, every single day.

Five years since his passing, Maradona remains omnipresent in this city. A sticker bearing his image smiles from a gutter, then not long afterwards, a man walks past and Diego’s face, tattooed on his bare arm, suddenly appears.

In another bar, there’s a more curious relic. “In 1986, I was in Milan for the match against AC,” explains the establishment’s owner, Bruno Alcidi. “When I boarded the plane, I realised Diego was travelling on it, too. As he stood up after landing, a tuft of his hair was lying on his seat. I took it, just to have a joke with friends at home.” He’s since used the hair as the centrepoint of his own tiny shrine, complete with photos of Maradona and a statue of the Virgin Mary.

As Alcidi speaks, the son of God is closer than he realises. On September 20, 1986, a baby by the name of Diego Armando Sinaglia was born in Naples. Today, that boy, now 38 years old, is back in the area for a brief visit.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He’s Maradona’s eldest child, born to Cristiana Sinagra, after a fling during a difficult period of the football great’s relationship with future wife Claudia Villafane. A long legal battle followed between Sinagra and Maradona – in 1993, little Diego was recognised by the court of Naples as Maradona’s son, his name officially changed to Diego Armando Maradona Jr.

As he peers out of the window of his black Mercedes outside his nearby residence – a series of terraced houses, with a guard at the entrance – the likeness to his dad is unmistakable. Same size, same facial expression. “Same tendency to put on weight, too,” he tells us. “Drive in and park your car, then we’ll take mine. I’d like to stop by the hairdressers to get a shave, then we’ll see where to eat.”

Married to wife Nunzia, with two children, Diego Matias and India Nicole, he may be descended from a deity, but he doesn’t act like it. “I’m a common guy – I’d like people to understand that,” he says. “I don’t have any kind of superpower. I don’t have anything more or less than other guys like me. I’m introverted by character, and I have a hard time relating to people I don’t know.”

No such worries at Costantino’s hairdressers in Quarto, a few miles west of the city, where he’s greeted warmly and immediately offered coffee. He’s long been a regular visitor here, just like some of Napoli’s finest players of the modern era. “Costantino is history in Naples, he invented Marek Hamsik’s mohawk,” Diego Jr explains. “Marek came here for eight years – so did many others like Piotr Zielinski and Allan.”

“I love Diego for his simplicity – I love him because he’s Diego, not because of his famous name,” Costantino says of his pal. “We got on from the first day we met.” Other customers have tattoos of Maradona Snr – on their shoulders, their thighs or their backs – and proudly show them to us.

In front of the shop, another Maradona mural has been painted by a local artist. “I think about my father a lot,” Diego Jr admits. “After he died, it hurt me to see his face in every corner of the city. Now I’ve got used to it, and it’s also comforting to know that people board a plane to Naples to bring him a flower. People’s affection has eased my pain a little.”

It wasn’t until 2003 that he was able to meet his father for the first time. Diego Sr finally recognised him as his son in 2007, after many years denying it. “For the person I am today, I owe it all to my mum, I grew up with her and my grandparents, but my father’s influence was also important at some points of my life,” he says.

“I was born Diego Armando Sinagra, but a few years later I was given the right to bear my father’s surname. I was six or seven. Bearing the name Maradona is peculiar, and I’ve often left Vodafone operators speechless when they call me. ‘What do you mean?’ they say. ‘Are you really Mr Maradona, or are you pulling my leg?’

“My childhood was good. We were not rich, but my grandparents and mum gave me everything I needed. I grew up in a common, working class family. My grandfather was a hairdresser and my grandmother was a beautician in his shop.

“My uncles loved me a lot – when I was born, my mother was 21, my aunt Francesca was 19, uncle Sasi was 17 and uncle Fabio was 15. They were like brothers to me, it was beautiful. My grandfather was like a father. In fact, he was more than that.”

Diego Jr agrees to drive into Naples for lunch – we choose a restaurant with a sea view near Castel Dell’Ovo. His family home is outside of the city these days, in Licola, and we quickly understand why – when he sits down, curious glances come from most tables around us. People have noticed him.

As soon as he stands up to make a phone call, a boy sitting at a nearby table asks him for a photo. When he wanders over to get some water, another approaches, too. “I told you I preferred to stay out of town,” Diego Jr tells us, when he sits back down with a smile.

He orders a hamburger with roast potatoes, and our chat quietly continues.

“The first clear memory I have of my father dates back to USA 94,” he explains. He was seven back then. “At that point, I really understood who he was, how important he was in football, and in general. I remember very well how he screamed into the camera after scoring against Greece. Although I have no personal recollection of it, I also know well about the two girls who escorted him off the pitch to doping control. USA 94 saw the greatest injustice in the history of football – both the 1990 and 1994 World Cups were basically stolen from him. I don’t have fond memories of that.”

Even though he wouldn’t meet his father for the first time until years later, Diego Jr had to live with the enormous expectations generated by his famous surname. He progressed as far as an appearance for Italy’s under 17 team in 2001, after several years in Napoli’s youth ranks, but the club went bankrupt in 2004.

That summer, he headed to Scotland for a trial with Dunfermline, but a deal couldn’t be agreed with his advisors. “We made an offer that we thought was fair for a laddie who hasn’t played for the first team,” Dunfermline’s director of football Jim Leishman said at the time. “But they thought it derisory, so we’re not going to pursue it.”

Instead he joined Genoa in Serie B, but didn’t feature for their first team as they were relegated to the third tier following a match-fixing scandal, despite 21 league goals from Diego Milito.

Soon, he was playing semi-professional football at regional level, with Servia, Internapoli, Quarto and Venafro. “People have often compared me to my father, but that’s superficial,” Diego Jr says. “He was unique, nothing compares to him. Why should I have compared myself? Just because I was his son? But Ludwig van Beethoven’s son didn’t play like his father, did he? They were two different people.”

His phone rings as we drink coffee. It’s Nunzia, who asks if we want to join her at Lido Varca d’Oro, a beach resort just a few minutes from their home, where she’d like to spend a sunny afternoon with their children. We decide to return to Licola, passing Napoli’s famous Stadio San Paolo, renamed the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in December 2020. “I always dreamed of playing with the Napoli jersey at the San Paolo,” Diego Jr says. “Today children dream of Real Madrid or Manchester City, but I was only in love with my club.”

He headed to the beach during his playing career, too: becoming an accomplished beach soccer star, scoring in the 2008 World Cup final against Brazil, then fittingly helping Napoli to their first ever Serie A title on the sand, just like his dad did on grass.

“My surname was a handicap for me, no doubt,” he says. “Sometimes I was told ‘If you wanted to avoid all this attention, all you had to do was not play football…’ But I wanted to because I loved it!

“I had my share of success too, in my small way. I made more than 100 appearances for the beach soccer national team, I played in two World Cups and two European Championships. It didn’t happen because of my name, or because of my father. I’m one of the 10 most prolific Italian beach soccer players of all time, and I also played football for Italy at youth level. It’s true, I wasn’t like Lionel Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo, nor did I get to play in Serie A, but that was partly because of my name.”

Happily, his relationship with his father grew closer – in 2016, the pair took to the field together in a charity match in Rome. “I’m very happy that I’ve been reunited with my son,” Maradona Sr said months earlier. “I love him a lot – he’s very like me.”

Even that brought challenges for Diego Jr, though. “It’s not easy for me to open up with people I’m not familiar with,” he admits. “That’s due to my story and also to the fact that, with a surname like mine, some people approach me with ulterior motives. I lost some of my childhood friends because I wouldn’t help them to take a picture with my father.”

Since his dad’s passing, he’s moved into coaching with lower league clubs Napoli United, Pompei and Montecalcio, spending much of this season managing Ibarra in Tenerife. “Today I very much love my life as a coach,” he says. “When I played myself, I thought that a manager had to be strict. I’m not like that now. It's difficult for me to define myself as a coach, but if I had to, I’d say that I’m honest with my boys.

“I hope that coaching is my future, but you must be able to reinvent yourself in life. I hope it doesn’t happen to me, but if I have to change path, I will. I don’t know how, but I will. Football has always been my life and I hope it continues to be so. My goal is to grow further.”

Approaching 40, he’s a man who’s increasingly at peace with himself, as the offspring of Diego Maradona. “Being his son is a source of pride for me – he made so many people happy,” Diego Jr says. “He was and still is an inspiration to so many people. He was a living legend, and in the years I was around him, he taught me so many things.

“For more than 25 years, he was a slave to cocaine. He didn’t always behave correctly, but who’s perfect in the end? I know he also said bad things about me over the years, but you have to put them into context. They have no value. At that time, my father was neither well nor clear-headed. I only judge him by what he said to me directly.”

The sun is sinking low behind the beach umbrellas to our left. A breeze has picked up and the late afternoon coolness begins to make itself felt. “Even with my mother, I’ve never talked this much,” he says.

Despite the perfect vista, it’s time for us to depart. As we do, Nunzia is lying on a sunbed with India Nicole, while Diego Jr sits on the sand, playing with Diego Matias. A normal family, and a normal dad, who just so happens to be the son of a footballing great.

Daniele Verri is an Italian journalist who writes for FourFourTwo as well as a number of other titles around the world, including BBC Sport . He has interviewed a wide range of footballers for FourFourTwo, including North Macedonia's history maker Goran Pandev, former Roma and Italy striker Vincenzo Montella and Brazilian goalkeeper Dida.

#1063. The four factors that make Brighton genuine Premier League title contenders

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

After beating Manchester City to continue a strong start, Richard Jolly explains why a Brighton title tilt is not as far-fetched as it might seem

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When Fabian Hurzeler was asked about Brighton’s possible participation in the title race, he tended to invoke Getafe in his answer. And if a club from Madrid are not exactly an opponent in the Premier League, this was Hurzeler’s version of an old cliché. He is taking it one game at a time, and Brighton & Hove Albion’s next game is against Getafe in the Europa Conference League.

More pertinently, though, their last one was away at Manchester City. They defeated the league leaders. Brighton’s last week has served as a barometer of their status against the established powers. They played well against Liverpool at Anfield, but lost 2-0. They twice led against City in the Carabao Cup, but went out on penalties. They beat them in the Premier League. For a club with plenty of high-profile scalps in recent years, the Etihad Stadium was the final frontier. They had won everywhere else of note. Now Hurzeler could maintain the pretence that the only thing on his mind was Getafe.

The unlikely challengers can deflect attention by citing the concerns they would have in other seasons. Eleven years ago, as Leicester City were an unexpected presence near the top of the table, Claudio Ranieri used to talk about targeting 40 points, even when it was clear Leicester would reach the usual barrier for safety with months to spare. Now Brighton are already halfway to the other mythical number, 38. Ranieri’s rhetoric was such that he could switch to meaningless but entertaining catchphrases; Hurzeler’s is less likely to spend spring saying “dilly ding, dilly dong”.

But the subject of a title tilt could become inescapable if Brighton extend their superb start. That seems possible: they have played the rest of the current top five and do not face any again until the return game with City in January. They don’t see Chelsea again until April, Liverpool or Arsenal until the final two games.

Is there a title decider there? History would suggest not. Brighton have never finished in the top five of the top flight. They often start seasons well – they had 21 points after 12 games in 2024-25, 13 after six in 2022-23, 12 after five in 2021-22 – but have a past of winless spells, too: under Hurzeler, they twice went six league matches without victory last season.

History suggests, too, that if Brighton are to upset the odds, it does not just depend upon their results. When Leicester were champions in 2016, it was facilitated by the failures of others, as no one else secured more than 71 points. Ranieri’s team earned 81. Now some of the supposed superpowers, Manchester United in particular, seem to be taking themselves out of contention. A sizeable punishment could rule City out. It is altogether harder to see Arsenal, in particular, from ending up with under 80 points.

Some elements indicate that Brighton should be taken seriously. One, oddly, lies in a couple of defeats: by losing their final two games of last season, they missed out on a Europa League spot. But the lighter load of the Conference League – both in its fixture list and lesser opponents – could equip them better for the Premier League.

Another lies in the firepower of Hurzeler’s team. Brighton are the top scorers in the division. They are expert at sharing the goals around: 16 players have found the net in all competitions, 11 of them in the Premier League. It is all the more remarkable as they have been without last season’s first-choice front three, with Danny Welbeck gone to Chelsea and Yankuba Minteh and Kaoru Mitoma yet to play in the top flight this season. With Minteh fit again and the prospect of Mitoma being back next month, Brighton could have more devastating wingers.

They have impressed defensively. They conceded four times to Chelsea, but only three other goals. Shutting City out gave them a sixth clean sheet of the season already, while they have only been breached once at home.

Luka Vuskovic has been outstanding, submitting an early application for the title of signing of the season. But a test for players being introduced to such a physical and demanding division as the Croatian defender and the 21-year-old midfielder Chema Andres is whether they can sustain that form for a whole campaign. The same question can be applied to the team as a whole and to veterans like Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk.

There are alternatives to each. The seeming strength of Brighton’s squad counts in their favour, even if it depends on Hurzeler continuing to pick the right option at the right time.

But certainly, with Brighton already five points clear of sixth place and seven ahead of seventh, they are unlikely to get a better chance to qualify for the Champions League. Yet as they continue to be an indictment of the elite, selling their best players at premium prices, replacing them, and continuing to prosper, they are indulging in a unique experiment. Can a selling club win the world’s richest league? We may find out in May.

It’s a secure way to bypass the resale lottery and walk straight into the ground with a prime view, making those "once-in-a-lifetime" derbies actually doable.

Chelsea's roller-coaster season has taken another turn in the last seven days - and not for the better.

After chalking up back-to-back wins over Bournemouth and Everton, Xabi Alonso's inconsistent side fell to a 2-0 home defeat against Tottenham Hotspur before seeing one of their three chances of silverware disappear as they lost to Liverpool on penalties in the Carabao Cup.

The Blues suffered their latest injury blow at Anfield as Maxence Lacroix was forced off with a hamstring injury, the centre back joining captain Reece James and striker Joao Pedro on the sidelines.

However, they will be boosted by the return of Cole Palmer after the England international served a one-match suspension following his red card against Spurs.

While Alonso could do with a victory after a tough week, his counterpart Michael Carrick surely has to win to keep his job as Manchester United manager.

The Old Trafford hierarchy decided to stick with the 45-year-old after Sunday's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth, which extended the Red Devils' winless run to eight matches in all competitions and left them just a point above the relegation zone.

Captain Bruno Fernandes was benched for that game as a result of his public criticism of Carrick's tactics after the 4-1 defeat by Como 10 days ago, but he could return after it was confirmed he would remain skipper following clear-the-air talks with the United boss.

Striker Benjamin Sesko will remain out for some time, though, while midfielder Kobbie Mainoo's involvement is in doubt.

The River Plate right back was joined by two security staff with riot shields as he departed the pitch following a challenge on Lautaro Blanco

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A fiery and ferocious Superclasico between Argentinian sides Boca Juniors and River Plate ended with riot shields as defender Gonzalo Montiel was escorted off the pitch by security staff following a late red card.

The biggest domestic match in Argentina’s Primera Division was littered with heavy tackles, physical altercations and interruptions as Boca Juniors secured a 1-0 victory at their home stadium of La Bombonera.

The tone was set in the first half as Lucas Martinez Quarta yanked the shirt of Boca striker Miguel Merentiel and was dismissed with a straight red card just 10 minutes into the match leaving River Plate with 10-men.

That intensified the raucous atmosphere inside La Bombonera and frustrations for the visitors grew when Lautaro Di Lollo sent Boca into the lead. Those frustrations boiled over again in the 79th minute as Montiel threw himself into a late challenge on Lautaro Blanco and received a second straight red card of the game reducing River Plate to nine players.

The right-back then taunted the vociferous home fans as he strode around the side of the pitch following his dismissal by pointing to himself, the River Plate badge on his shirt and making a spinning motion with his index finger, clearly referencing the two finals that River Plate won against Boca Juniors in 2018.

He also departed with a full smile and grin at the baying Boca supporters whose response was to launch projectiles from the stands at the defender.

Montiel was quickly approached by two security staff in riot gear who guided him to safety. Their riot shields were needed multiple times as they shielded the River Plate player from a variety of thrown objects including beer cans.

The game was a difficult one for referee Nicolas Ramirez who has come under criticism for his quick dismissal’s of River Plate players without affording the same considerations to Boca Juniors’ stars. Blanco, who was fouled by Montiel, had previously only been shown a yellow card for similar tackle on Tobias Andrada while Nicolas Paredes escaped a second yellow and Di Lollo was reprieved for a shirt pull inside the box on Nicolas Otamendi - a similar incident to Martinez Quarta’s previous red card offence.

#1060. UK students call for school uniforms to be banned in pornography

Short skirts, knee-high socks, white blouses: Girls' school uniform items are widely used as costumes in pornographic videos. As students experience harassment, a group wants to change that.

Aylin and Mae, both age 15, are members of their school's Little Feminist Book Club in Bicester, Oxfordshire, England.

During a group discussion, the club learned that teenagers at other schools were trying to have the sale of school uniforms banned in sex shops.

Schoolgirl costumes are also widely used in pornographic videos.

"All of us unanimously agreed. We wanted to take it a step further; we wanted to ban school uniform from all pornography," Aylin told DW. As a result, they started a petition to raise awareness of the issue.

Many of their fellow students, as the petition states, have already had unpleasant experiences while wearing their uniforms. Some reported being harassed as early as the age of 11. Many of these experiences had left them feeling frightened, ashamed and insecure. "I don't wear my school uniform outside of school," said Mae. "I don't like wearing it out."

In their petition, the girls also refer to a 2018 report by the charity Plan International. According to a survey in the report, 35% of the 1,004 respondents aged 14 to 21 had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing a school uniform. Eight percent said they had been filmed or photographed by a stranger without their permission, or that someone had taken a photo under their school skirt, known as "upskirting."

"Something that should actually be innocent, something that is supposed to symbolize a community, has now become discredited in society," said Mae. "And our perception of what a school uniform represents has been distorted by this disgusting media."

School uniforms are common in many countries around the world. They are meant to make class and financial divides less visible, which is also supposed to prevent bullying while strengthening a community feeling.

In the United Kingdom, uniforms are mandatory at almost all schools and preschools, which means essentially all children between the ages of 4 to 16 wear them.

Outside school, children have no way to escape unwanted attention.

"We just want to prevent people from thinking about children and school uniforms in that way," said Mae. "Hopefully, we'll be able to actually turn the ban into legislation."

Until that happens, they still have a long way to go, but the girls are optimistic. As of October 5, 2026, the petition has garnered more than 24,000 signatures. Thanks to an article in the English newspaper The Times, it's also gotten plenty of attention.

Now, Mae and Aylin hope to get parliament to debate the issue. Two Members of Parliament have already voiced their support.

But the girls also know some people believe longer skirts are the solution. "I believe that's wrong," explains Aylin. "We shouldn't blame the victims. We should blame those who think it is acceptable to sexualize them."

This article was originally written in German.

Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert

Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert

The Rub’ al Khali is the world’s largest sand sea, covering almost a third of the Arabian peninsula.

The desert, whose name translates to The Empty Quarter, was once part of the lush savannah known as ‘Green Arabia’ – the periodic blooming of the region as ice age climatic shifts brought more rainfall.

Evidence of ancient humans abounds in the regions around the desert, but an expedition into the interior has returned empty handed. The surprising absence of stone tools and other signs of human occupation has led archaeologists to a new theory of the factors governing human migration, that ancient peoples needed not just water to settle, but stone as well.

The England midfielder hails from the Channel Islands
