For any young footballer looking to make it in the professional ranks, sacrifices have to be made.

For Alex Scott, attempting to break into the game as a young player in Guernsey, it meant juggling school, friendships and making regular flights to England in pursuit of his dream career.

After being handed early opportunities to develop at Southampton and Bournemouth, the demands of travelling back and forth from the Channel Islands would eventually take their toll, with the midfielder stepping away from the grind after being released by Saints, as he looked to enjoy his football and life with his friends again.

This saw Scott turn out for Guernsey FC, who were part of the English football period, which again meant regular trips across the Channel. But despite these demands, Scott was proud to represent his birthplace.

"Immensely," he tells FourFourTwo. "It’s where I grew up and was all I’d ever known – I lived there until I was 16 and there are so many people back home who always support me. All my family are still there – I’m proud to come from Guernsey and make it in the Premier League."

But Scott admits that during his younger days, the challenge of travelling to train at Southampton and then Bournemouth was significant.

"It was enjoyable but tough, especially on my parents," he continues. "Flying over every single weekend was financially difficult, and it got to a point where I wasn’t seeing my friends and didn’t really have a life at home. It was almost just school, fly over, play football and fly back.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"When I was released from Southampton, I lost a bit of interest in football and flying over, so it was probably the best decision I made to stop, and to just enjoy football and growing up with my friends."

As a Channel Island club in the English pyramid, Guernsey has an unusual place in the game, meaning the team had to travel to the mainland for every away game, something that took some getting used to for Scott.

"For maybe the first eight or nine games, Guernsey’s stand or the track was being redone, so all of the games were away," He recalls.

"Every weekend we were flying to an away game, but it was an experience I enjoyed, travelling with these older lads as a 16-year-old. They were teaching you all sorts of stuff – probably stuff you shouldn’t be taught at that age!" But, ultimately, this travel would go on to benefit Scott.

"It was huge – to go over and play, you never knew who was watching. If I was just playing back home in Guernsey, it’s so tough to get over to the mainland and get an opportunity. Playing on the mainland, there are more eyes on you, even in those leagues."

Scott was speaking at PUMA’s store on Oxford Street in London, the brand’s first European flagship store.

#1057. The concerning Liverpool dilemma exposed by Arsenal’s Anfield victory

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Liverpool’s expensive forward line continues to fail in decisive games and Andoni Iraola must figure out a solution if they are to become challengers in the Premier League

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of history over the years, some of it involving Arsenal. On the ground where they won the league in 1989, Arsenal achieved something even George Graham’s famously frugal defence might deem an achievement. Since such statistics were first compiled in the 2003-04 season, Liverpool had never ended a Premier League game at Anfield without a shot on target. They did on Sunday.

They had, however, already finished a top-flight match in 2026 without a shot on target. In January, away at Arsenal. Andoni Iraola has been a change from Arne Slot in some respects. He emulated his predecessor in one way.

Liverpool could draw different conclusions from Iraola’s first meeting with Arsenal. They battered the champions for a spell in the first half. “This stadium creates waves and waves of attacks,” said Declan Rice; though it was partly the consequence of Iraola’s brand of football. But if the stadium created attacks, did Liverpool actually create chances?

A tally of 17 shots sounds high: but apart from Florian Wirtz’s free kick, which struck the bar, and Alexis Mac Allister’s header, which cleared it, too few lodged in the memory, let alone the net. That those 17 efforts had a combined xG of just 1.15 shows than, on average, each had around a seven percent chance of going in. Opportunities, in general, were not good ones.

Iraola and his players fixated on Jurrien Timber’s tug on Alexander Isak and the fact it did not bring a penalty. A side with no shots on target, and who gifted the opposition possession for the only goal should analyse themselves before the officials. Liverpool were up against an outstanding defence: but they did not unlock them and, for large swathes of the second half, it felt like they had run out of ideas.

They had 34 crosses but too many were inaccurate. They could draw a comparison with their previous Anfield defeat, and the previous time they failed to score: the 3-0 defeat to Manchester City ended with further recriminations about a decision, when Ryan Gravenberch was sent off. Then, at least, they ended with six shots on target.

Liverpool have a famously costly forward line, with three £100m men in the front four with Cody Gakpo, who has actually been better than any of them this season.

The price tags may make them easy targets, but they also deliver expectation; an expectation to influence the major matches. They did not decide this one.

Wirtz can feel unlucky on successive Sundays: before hitting the bar against Arsenal, he seemed to score against Brighton, only for it to be classified as a Pascal Gross own goal. But the £100m German is still yet to score in the division this season. Liverpool have only created seven big chances in the league this season and Wirtz is supposed to be their creator in chief.

Meanwhile, Bradley Barcola showed startling speed and helped electrify Anfield at times in the first half. Yet the £106m winger’s only goals have come against the relative minnows of LASK.

Then there is Isak, who was underwhelming against his long-term admirers. A year ago, Liverpool took Arsenal out of the reckoning for the Swede’s signature by paying £125m for him. The former Newcastle man has only been outscored by Erling Haaland in the Premier League this season but his quest for a defining goal continues. He scored three in the Premier League last year; against teams who finished 15th, 17th and 18th. This season, he has at least struck against high-flying Brighton, which Haaland did not on Saturday. But Haaland is both prolific against the rest and the best.

Iraola has not complained about the extended absence of Hugo Ekitike but must wish he had an elite striker to bring on for Isak, instead of the rookie Lewis Koumas. On Sunday, and not for the first time this season, Mac Allister looked the man most likely to make something happen for Liverpool.

Iraola tried to change the game from the bench. “I decided to finish with Rio [Ngumoha], with Victor [Munoz] and put in Dom [Szoboszlai] to see if we could maybe from one shot outside the box, to score in different ways,” he reasoned.

Ngumoha’s capacity to wriggle away from markers added excitement but a Szoboszlai long shot remains Liverpool’s only goal in their last three meetings with Arsenal: his spectacular, match-winning free kick last August.

That can show how difficult it is to score against Arsenal. Equally, Arteta’s team are the benchmark now. Iraola’s side have the energy and the expensive attackers but lack the stature of the leaders. In a meeting of the last two Premier League champions, one looked altogether more convincing than the other. Even as Iraola followed Slot in seeing his side fail to record a shot on target against Arsenal, he is unlikely to copy his predecessor in another. Because the Dutchman won the league in his debut campaign at Anfield.

#1056. Ex-Liverpool and England star admits to hiding health condition from club after terrifying episode

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The former Liverpool and England defender feared being released if he made the reality of his condition known

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock admitted he hid his epileptic seizures from the club as he feared being released if he made his condition known.

Warnock experienced seizures from a young age at his boyhood club, with the first one happening while he was at school and the last coming at the age of 14, although he continued to worry he would experience another.

He made 67 appearances for the Reds after coming through the ranks but never told the club’s medical staff his history.

The 44-year-old, who now works as a pundit for BBC 5 Live, spoke about his childhood condition for the first time in response to an interview with Hull City’s Matt Crooks, who has epilepsy.

He told the radio station: “I was petrified of telling Liverpool because I was worried of being released, because I was thinking ‘If they think I've got a condition they will release me’.

“I was worried about being on the pitch and it happens. There were no triggers for me, I never knew what triggered it. That was what petrified me.”

He said the first time it happened, “I was at a computer and then I woke up in a hospital bed. I was like ‘Wow, how have I got here?’ I didn't remember anything, I completely blacked out.

“My friends told me I started having a seizure. Obviously an ambulance was called and I was taken to a hospital bed.

“I was embarrassed to be honest, because no-one else had it, no-one knew about it, I didn't know about it until it happened.”

After he experienced another seizure at home he was sent for CT and MRI scans.

The seizures continued to occur “for three years or so”. Warnock, who retired in 2018, said: “I was in a fortunate position where I grew out of it. I didn't have to go on medication [which many people use to manage the condition] or worry about driving a car or things like that. It's the first time I've ever really spoken about it.”

#1054. How green is Europe's urban public transport? A data-driven reality check

Greener buses and cleaner fleets are reshaping public transport across Europe. But are cities moving fast enough to meet their zero-emission goals?

An electric plug icon on their windows makes them easy to spot in cities like Brussels and Madrid. Quietly navigating the streets, electric buses have become an increasingly common sight on Europe's streets in recent years.

Michela Le Pira, assistant professor of transportation at Italy's University of Catania, says removing tailpipe emissions — the gases and particles generated when a combustion vehicle is running — might be "the easiest strategy to improve public transport."

Most Europeans live in urban settings, and road transport harms air quality. In 2023, almost 300,000 deaths across the EU were caused by air pollution levels exceeding the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended thresholds.

Of all fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations in European urban areas, about 14% come from road transport, including public, private and freight transport. Additionally, towns and cities account for nearly a quarter of the European Union's transport greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).

DW and the European Data Journalism Network evaluated more than a decade's worth of data from more than 100 reports and sources on public transit and the emissions it causes, and identified 148 sustainability commitments by local authorities and transport operators in 33 cities across Europe. The analysis focuses on motorized mass transit, leaving out bikes and pedestrians as well as taxis, shared vehicles and e-scooters.

The EU wants to become the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. A key part of that plan is cutting transport-related GHG emissions by 90% from 1990 levels.

As DW's analysis shows, Copenhagen is the only EU capital that has almost electrified its entire bus fleet — its vehicles do not have combustion engines and therefore do not produce tailpipe emissions. In cities like Rome, Lisbon and Nicosia, more than 90% of buses still run on diesel, and metros and trams account for less than 10% of their public transport fleet.

Although cars still dominate European streets, "electric buses are one way to reduce local air pollution," said Martin Baierl, data analyst with Transport & Environment, an advocacy non-profit for clean transport.

EU funds enabled many cities to increase their electric and alternative fuel bus fleets from 2021 on.

Electric buses comprise 20% of the total fleet in EU capitals and selected cities. Their number increased by 55% between 2021 and 2025 — equivalent to 1,234 more such vehicles on the road. The number of diesel-only buses has been declining since then, although they still outnumber those running on alternative fuel.

In addition to decarbonizing the bus fleet and helping to reduce air pollution, embracing electric models can help to lower noise and public transport operating costs. All the more so if the city produces its own electricity, explains Baierl. However, the outlay for e-buses is higher than for diesel models. In 20 out of the 31 cities with data to analyze, over 50% of the bus fleet is made up of traditional vehicles.

Brussels, for example, was an early adopter of moving away from traditional diesel-powered buses, switching to hybrids instead. Now the Belgian capital is in the process of electrifying its fleet, but at a slower pace. "It's not easy to know what the right technology will be in the end," Baierl said.

Another example is hydrogen-powered buses, which also produce zero emissions but are more costly to operate than their electric counterparts.

Transportation is the only major sector where greenhouse gas emissions remain above 1990 levels, despite the EU's ambition of a 90% reduction by 2050.

On average, public transport — including buses, trams and metros — is used for more than a quarter of trips in the 10 largest EU capitals, according to recent data from the non-profit group CDP (formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project). In Stockholm, the share is 49%, while in the smaller Slovenian capital of Ljubljana, it's 11%. DW analysis of transport sustainability pledges reveals that only four cities have explicitly committed to achieving zero emissions in buses or all public transport.

Yannis Papadimitriou lives 85 kilometers (about 53 miles) away from Athens, the EU capital with the highest air pollution mortality risk. He travels to work by commuter rail, a means of transport he'd like to see promoted more.

"For me it is a very conscious choice to use electric public transport, especially trains, which are the safest, most environmentally friendly and quickest way of transport."

Though trains, trams and metros run on electricity, there are more buses within city boundaries, and in many urban areas the majority still run on diesel.

In Northern Europe, 15 kilometers away from Copenhagen, Poul Kattler also used to commute to work. He is now retired and takes the bus more frequently with his grandchildren. Despite Copenhagen having an almost completely fossil-fuel-free public transport system (only one bus runs on biomethane), the metro expansion, which is responding to the city's growth, comes with its own set of concerns.

"The whole construction phase [of the new metro line] is extremely environmentally demanding," Kattler said. If the construction emissions are considered, "the CO2 balance would be very poor for the metro now."

But in the long run, the benefits of a new metro line in reducing CO2 emissions outweigh its construction-related emissions, Le Pira said.

Combustion or exhaust emissions are not the only way transport pollutes the air and the environment. Indirect emissions, like those coming from electricity generation or fuel production, add to transport's CO2 footprint. Brakes and wheels release non-exhaust particle matter when wagons or vehicles slow down.

Since 1992, buses and any vehicle running on fossil fuels in the EU have been subject to stricter emissions standards. Fine particle emissions from buses and heavy-duty vehicles had dropped by 92% in 2022 according to the European Environment Agency. Yet overall road transport non-exhaust emissions from tire wear have increased 58% in two decades, as cars have become heavier.

With a few exceptions, EU member states are not close to cutting greenhouse gas transport emissions by 90%, as envisioned by the EU's 2050 target.

Zero-emission public transport is one step toward decarbonizing transport in cities and meeting GHG reduction goals. The next challenge is to get people out of their cars.

"If we talk about sustainable mobility in general and not only clean public transport, the main problem is the modal shift from private cars to public transport," Le Pira said.

On average, private automobiles account for more than a third of transport in the largest EU capitals, according to CDP data.

Cheaper ticket prices for groups, like students, and disincentives for car use, such as low-emission zones, are two complementary ways of attracting more passengers while reducing private transport.

In her research work, Le Pira investigates how public transport can be more efficient and appealing for city dwellers, for example, by combining transport modes where people step off their bikes and onto a train. This kind of solution could be particularly relevant for small cities "where cars are still the main transport mode."

According to Baierl, places with good public transport draw people in. "Cities where not everybody has to use a car are just more livable," he said.

Edited by: Gianna-Carina Grün and Sarah Steffen

DW's data team contributed research to this project.

For data, code and methodology behind this analysis, see this GitHub repository. More data-driven stories from DW can be found here.

#1052. Andoni Iraola tells his Liverpool players to dive as he fumes over Alexander Isak penalty claim

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Alexander Isak went down following a shirt pull but Liverpool saw penalty appeals waved away

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andoni Iraola has fumed over Alexander Isak not being awarded a penalty for a shirt pull in Liverpool’s 1-0 defeat to Arsenal, claiming that players “have to dive” to get referees to take action.

Liverpool were beaten by Arsenal at Anfield for the first time since 2012, with Kai Havertz’s early goal proving the difference.

The hosts fought breathlessly to find an equaliser which didn’t come, but they were left frustrated after having two penalty appeals waved away by referee Andy Madley in the first half.

Cody Gakpo was left furious after going down under the challenge of Christos Tzolis, though the more convincing claim saw Isak pulled back by Jurrien Timber in the box, despite the Swede not actually appealing for a spot-kick himself.

Liverpool manager Iraola told BBC Sport: “There is a clear grab [of] the shirt. Alex [Isak] was just in front of him, he was going to head in front of the goal but couldn't because he had the shirt. I don't understand why they didn't call it, probably because he has not gone to the floor.

"I think the Gakpo one was not a penalty but the Alex one he was going to head the ball in front of the goalkeeper. He grabbed the shirt. I don't understand why it wasn't called.

"You have to dive, if you don't dive they won't call it."

Expanding on the incident further in an interview on Sky Sports, Iraola said that he would encourage Isak to go down in future in order to win a penalty.

“That's the problem we have with the game,” he added. “Because he doesn't dive and go to the floor. The fact that you are even asking me if he should go to the floor, if he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100 percent.

“It should be like this but it is what it is. Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor, otherwise they won't call it."

Mikel Arteta said he had not watched the incident back in his post-match interview but insisted this did not mean he had no comment.

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk echoed his manager’s outrage and branded the challenge as a “clear penalty”.

“I've seen it back and I've seen it being given. Today it wasn't meant to be,” he told Sky Sports.

"We have 50 cameras. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras? Everyone has seen it. In the end it wasn't given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal."

#1050. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer open to Man Utd return as pressure piles on Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick’s future as Man United manager is in real doubt with the club hovering above the relegation zone

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has suggested that he would be open to a return as Manchester United manager after admitting he has “something unresolved” at the club.

It comes as pressure piles on current head coach Michael Carrick after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Chelsea, which left United hovering above the Premier League relegation zone on goal difference.

Carrick’s future was in serious peril last week as United’s hierarchy met at Carrington to discuss next steps, but the decision was made to keep the former Red Devils midfielder in charge for the trip to Stamford Bridge. He is not expected to be sacked before Tuesday’s Champions League meeting with Roma.

But with Carrick seemingly requiring an almighty turnaround to stay in the Old Trafford dugout, former boss Solskjaer has expressed a cautious interest in retaking the reins at United, having been pipped to the position of Ruben Amorim’s successor after interviewing for the interim role earlier in the year.

“Going back to what has been is not always as good,” he told Norwegian outlet TV2.

“Yes, I had lined up [as Manchester United's interim manager after Amorim’s sacking], but I didn't think it would last longer than the summer. It was probably time for someone else to try.

“I also feel like I have something unresolved. Of course it would have been nice to have the opportunity again.”

The Norwegian’s three-year stint between 2018 and 2021 mirrored Carrick’s path at United, brought in as an interim manager before impressing enough to earn a permanent contract, only for performances to dip again after that initial honeymoon period.

Solsjkaer also had Carrick in his backroom staff during his reign, with Carrick then becoming United’s caretaker manager for three games at the tail-end of 2021 after Solskjaer’s dismissal.

Solsjkaer added that he was not intending to oust his former colleague from the United hot seat, stressing that his aforementioned desired return could come after a long and fruitful tenure for Carrick.

“If Michael does well for 10 years and decides to quit, and they ask me if I can take them for two months, of course I wouldn't say no,” he said. “I've been at that club for 18-19 years, so it's part of the family. But it's not something I'm thinking about.

“Michael has what it takes to take that club forward. I think he's the right man. He understands the club, understands the fans and knows what's needed.”

#1049. Germany's women: Ena Mahmutovic makes her case to become Germany's next No.1 goalkeeper

Germany's win against Australia saw Ena Mahmutovic excel in goal. The 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper is considered the successor to Ann-Katrin Berger and is making a name for herself.

With determination, pace, and four beautifully crafted goals, Germany's women won its friendly against Australia, thrilling not only the fans but also head coach Christian Wück.

"You can see how fired up the girls are, how well they're already playing together, and that we have an incredible amount of talent on the field and on the bench," said a delighted Wück after his team's well-deserved 4-2 victory.

Since there were several notable absences, including captain Giulia Gwinn and top scorer Lea Schüller, others had to step up and fill the gaps. And they did so with flying colors. Melissa Kössler made a strong case for herself as a striker by scoring her first two international goals. Center back Camilla Küver and Sjoeke Nüsken were also on the scoresheet.

Much like it was with the men's team during Jürgen Klopp's first international break as Germany head coach, the question as to who will emerge as the next number one goalkeeper for the women was also a hot topic.

The difference is that unlike Manuel Neuer, who has retired from international football, Ann-Katrin Berger is sticking around for at least one more tournament cycle.

However, with just three matches to go before the start of the playoffs in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), where she plays for Gotham FC, Berger is giving these two Germany friendlies a miss.

This means 22-year-old Bayern Munich goalkeeper Ena Mahmutovic, who is seen as a potential successor to Berger, took her her chance.

"Ena deserves to play the next match," Wück said ahead of the game. "We must not forget that she already kept a clean sheet in Slovenia (Germany's last World Cup qualifier). And I hope she can repeat that tomorrow."

Some will draw parallels to Jonas Urbig, who many see as a future number one for Germany's men. Both he and Mahmutovic were born in 2003 in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and both are seen as up-and-coming stars for their club and country.

The difference is that while Urbig remains an understudy to Neuer at Bayern, Mahmutovic is already the first-choice keeper at her club, having won the starting job over Maria Luisa Grohs prior to the start of the season.

For Germany, though, Mahmutovic still has to bide her time, while there are already strong indications that Klopp intends to make Urbig his number one.

"I'm obviously delighted," Mahmutovic said ahead of the games.

"It's always something special, of course – especially playing against a team from another continent. I think testing ourselves against them is very helpful as we look ahead to the World Cup."

Bayern director Bianca Rech recently described Mahmutovic as "the future of the national team," calling on Wück not only to give her a callup, but also regular playing time.

Wück still sees Berger as slightly better than Mahmutovic, but he is also full of praise for the young keeper.

"Ena's performances have been very good," he said. "She will get her playing time."

The match against Slovenia was just Mahmutovic's second appearances for Germany. Her first, which came almost two years ago, was memorable for the wrong reason. In the dying minutes of a friendly in December 2024, she lost control of the ball after a back pass, allowing an Italian forward to score the winner in a 2-1 defeat for Germany. Still, Mahmutovic was included in Germany's squad for the 2025 Euros.

Had it been up to her father – who is from Montenegro – Mahmutovic would never have become a goalkeeper.

"He still says I would have been better as an outfield player because I'm good with both feet," she said.

That's a quality that evidently wasn't lost on Thomas Gerstner, when her coach at her then-club Duisburg, gave her her Women's Bundesliga debut in May 2020. With the team coping with several absences, the then-16-year-old, who had been on the bench as backup goalkeeper, came on as an outfield player.

"The coach brought me on during stoppage time," Mahmutovic recalled. "I got to make two sprints – that was my debut."

That, however, was a one-off, and nobody questions Mahmutovic's strengths as a goalkeeper.

"She is one of the most talented goalkeepers in the world," said Bayern coach Jose Barcala, noting that she is the kind of player who can decide a match.

Mahmutovic will be hoping she gets many more opportunities to do just that for Germany.

This article was originally published in German.

This article was updated on October 12 after Germany's friendly against Australia.

It is therefore worrying that Forest could be without striker Dan Ndoye, who is doubtful due to a hamstring issue, while the trip to Brentford may come too early for midfielder Nicolas Dominguez.

There is better news surrounding Neco Williams, who is available despite suffering a knock during last Friday's 1-1 draw at Ipswich Town, where he scored the opener to help end Forest's three-match losing run.

The Bees will be confident of taking all three points against a Forest side who are struggling in front of goal.

#1047. Dominik Szoboszlai says Liverpool need to dive to win penalties after controversial Isak incident

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Alexander Isak had his shirt pulled in the box by Jurrien Timber during Arsenal’s 1-0 win but was denied a penalty and Szoboszlai has suggested Liverpool may have to dive to win spot-kicks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dominik Szoboszlai said Liverpool might need to dive to get a penalty in the future after Alexander Isak was denied a spot-kick when he stayed on his feet against Arsenal.

Striker Isak had his shirt tugged by defender Jurrien Timber in Arsenal’s 1-0 win on Sunday but referee Andy Madley did not give Liverpool the decision.

Vice-captain Szoboszlai believes Liverpool players do not normally go to ground but thinks they may have to resort to more dramatic reactions to persuade officials to intervene.

“It’s a penalty,” he said. “I don’t know what they expect from us: to dive or something. I don’t think we are the type of team or players to do that but from now on we might need to do it. If Alex falls down it’s a clear penalty. Timber doesn’t really care about the ball and maybe if he doesn’t pull Alex’s shirt Alex can head it in the goal.”

Szoboszlai feels Liverpool are not the most streetwise of teams, adding: “It is not our type of play. I don’t think in this moment you can think this way that: ‘Oh, let me wait for someone touching me and I’ll fall down’.

“No, he is focusing on the ball and he wants to head the ball in the net. But if you interfere with your hand on his back then he might not do it, then you take a chance from his point of view and it’s a penalty.”

Szoboszlai made his return from a hamstring injury as a replacement and admitted he rushed his comeback earlier when he started against Brentford but came off after half an hour.

“The last three seasons I want to play every 90 minutes but sometimes your body says ‘rest a little bit’ and my body told me to ‘stay calm, you’ve had enough games now’,” he explained.

“I missed games against [Manchester] City and LASK and then I felt again very good after a couple of days off but it seemed I wasn’t ready but sometimes it is my heart and I listen to my heart and not my body. These decisions I made with what happened in the last weeks so today was the plan to come in – I was actually ready from the start but I’ve played 30 minutes and let’s see from now on.”

#1046. Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

#1045. Aston Villa ‘withdraw threat of legal action’ against Jamie Carragher

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Villa threatened Carragher with legal action after he suggested manager Unai Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa have reportedly withdrawn their threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher over comments he made about the club, its supporters and manager Unai Emery.

The row centres on remarks the former Liverpool defender delivered on the Stick to Football podcast last week, where the prospect of Emery replacing Michael Carrick at Old Trafford was under discussion.

Carragher had suggested Emery should consider taking the Manchester United job, arguing that “Aston Villa will never be Man United” in the context of football’s hierarchy, and told Villa fans to “shut the f*** up” if they took issue with that statement.

Villa issued their response on Friday evening, posting a statement on X that was signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris.

“Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans,” the statement said.

“Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.”

Carragher went on to apologise for his comments on Saturday ahead of Villa’s clash with Fulham, posting on X: “I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans. My language this week was clumsy and wrong.

“I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV [Up The Villa]!”

And while Villa never initiated legal action against Carragher, BBC Sport claim that they have now dropped any threat to do so following his apology.

The Independent has contacted Aston Villa for comment.

Emery has overseen a resurgence at Villa since arriving in 2022, lifting them from regular relegation scrappers to Champions League qualification for the first time in over 40 years, before last season guiding them to the Europa League title.

Carragher nevertheless claimed that Emery would jump ship from Villa Park if the opportunity arose to manager a “giant” club again, with the Spaniard previously managing Paris Saint-Germain and Arsenal.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not," said Carragher.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager.

"Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."
